rw: Bankruptcy is a court process that lets people or businesses who cannot repay their debts get relief by discharging or restructuring what they owe.

ww.A tax credit for people who owe a great: A tax credit reduces tax owed and has nothing to do with court proceedings for debts that someone is unable to repay.
ww.A savings plan for people who want to bu: A savings plan builds wealth over time, which is the opposite of bankruptcy, a legal remedy used after debts become unmanageable.
ww.A type of loan offered to people with po: Bankruptcy is not a loan product at all, and poor-credit loans are just borrowing, not a court process for debt relief.

rw: Federal loans come with government protections such as income-driven repayment, deferment and forgiveness options, while private loan terms are set by each lender.

ww.Private loans always have lower rates th: Private loans do not always cost less, since rates depend on credit history, and federal rates are fixed by law and often lower.
ww.They are identical in every respect, wit: Federal and private loans differ a lot, because federal loans have government-set rates and protections while private terms vary by lender.
ww.Federal loans never need repayment, what: Federal loans must still be repaid, though repayment can be adjusted or deferred, so saying they never need repayment is false.

rw: FAFSA stands for Free Application for Federal Student Aid, the form used to apply for federal grants, work-study and student loans.

ww.Free Account for Financial Savings Accou: This invents a savings account meaning, but FAFSA is an aid application and has nothing to do with opening savings accounts.
ww.Funds for Americans' Student Aid fund: This names a made-up fund, but FAFSA is an application form for federal aid, not a pool of money for Americans.
ww.Federal Agency for Financial Student Acc: FAFSA is not a federal agency, and the word Application in the real name shows it is a form rather than an agency.

rw: A scholarship is money awarded for education based on merit, need or other criteria, and it does not have to be repaid.

ww.A credit card with a rewards program att: A credit card with rewards is a borrowing tool for purchases and carries no connection to money awarded to pay for education.
ww.A student loan that must be repaid with: A student loan has to be repaid with interest, whereas a scholarship is a gift of money that never needs repayment.
ww.A tax on students who attend college eac: Scholarships are awards paid to students, not a tax charged on them, so this reverses the actual meaning of the word.

rw: A grant is money given for education or a project by a government or organization, and it typically does not have to be repaid.

ww.A credit line that must be repaid in ful: A credit line repaid in full with interest describes a loan, while a grant is money given that normally needs no repayment.
ww.A loan with interest that must be repaid: A loan repaid in installments with interest describes borrowing, which is the opposite of a grant that does not usually require repayment.
ww.A tax that students pay on the money the: Grants are not taxes charged to students; they are gifts of money for education, so this describes a levy instead.

rw: A lease is a contract giving someone the right to use property, such as an apartment or car, for a set period in exchange for payments.

ww.A loan to buy stock in a company that is: Buying stock is an investment in a company, whereas a lease is a rental agreement for using property such as a car or apartment.
ww.Buying with cash at the time of sale, pa: Paying the full price in cash at the time of sale is an outright purchase, while a lease is use of property over time.
ww.A tax form that must be filed by every r: A tax form is a government filing, but a lease is a contract between owner and user, and renters are not all required to file one.

rw: Leasing builds no ownership, because you only pay to use the car, and mileage caps with penalties are common, which are real downsides.

ww.Unlimited mileage on every trip you take: Leases usually cap annual mileage and charge fees for going over, so unlimited mileage is not a downside and is generally not offered.
ww.You always own the car, as the lease pas: With a lease you do not own the car, since title stays with the lessor unless you buy it at the end of the term.
ww.No monthly payments are required on a le: Leased cars require regular monthly payments, so claiming none are required is false and would not be a downside of leasing anyway.

rw: A down payment is the portion of the purchase price paid upfront in cash, which lowers the amount that must be borrowed.

ww.A late fee charged on a payment made aft: A late fee is a penalty for paying after the due date, and it is unrelated to the upfront money paid at purchase.
ww.The final payment on a loan or a lease c: The final payment on a loan is a payoff or balloon payment made at the end, whereas a down payment is made at the start.
ww.Interest charged on a loan by the lender: Interest is the lender's yearly charge for borrowing, and it is paid over time rather than as an upfront share of the price.

rw: Ten percent of $200,000 is 0.10 times 200,000, which equals $20,000, so that is the required down payment on the home.

ww.$180,000: $180,000 is 90 percent of the home price, which is the amount financed after a 10 percent down payment, not the down payment itself.
ww.$200,000: $200,000 is the entire price of the home, which would be a 100 percent down payment, not the 10 percent required here.
ww.$2,000: $2,000 is only 1 percent of $200,000, so it comes from misplacing the decimal point when taking 10 percent of the price.

rw: PMI protects the lender if the borrower defaults, and it is typically required when the down payment is less than 20 percent.

ww.Insurance for the house against fire, wi: Insurance on the house against fire, wind and theft is homeowners insurance, which protects the property, while PMI protects the lender.
ww.Insurance for the borrower's death, payi: Insurance that pays off a mortgage when the borrower dies is mortgage life insurance, a different product from PMI, which covers lender default risk.
ww.A tax on mortgages that lenders collect: PMI is an insurance premium paid by the borrower, not a government tax, and lenders collect it only to protect themselves.

rw: A fixed-rate mortgage keeps the same interest rate for the entire term, so the principal and interest payment stays predictable throughout the loan.

ww.A loan with no interest charged to the b: Every loan charges interest, and a fixed-rate mortgage does too, so a loan with no interest charged at any time is wrong.
ww.A loan for a car that is paid back in eq: A car loan paid in equal parts describes an installment loan for a vehicle, which is not the definition of a home mortgage.
ww.A loan whose rate changes with the marke: A rate that changes with the market describes an adjustable-rate mortgage, which is the opposite of a fixed-rate loan.

rw: An ARM starts with an initial rate for a set period, then the rate adjusts periodically based on a market index.

ww.A loan with a fixed rate for the whole l: A rate that stays fixed for the whole term describes a fixed-rate mortgage, which is the opposite of an adjustable-rate loan.
ww.A loan with no rate attached to it at an: Every mortgage carries an interest rate, so a loan with no rate at all cannot be an adjustable-rate mortgage.
ww.A loan for a car with a rate that can ne: An ARM is a home loan whose rate can change, so a car loan whose rate never changes does not describe it.

rw: Home equity is what the owner actually holds in the property, calculated as the current value of the home minus the mortgage balance still owed.

ww.The property tax paid each year to the c: Property tax is a yearly charge paid to local government, and it is a cost of owning a home rather than the owner's stake.
ww.The mortgage amount that you still owe o: The mortgage amount still owed is the debt against the home, which is subtracted from value to find equity rather than being equity.
ww.The down payment only, the sum paid at t: The down payment is only the starting part of equity, because equity also grows as principal is paid and as the home appreciates.

rw: Equity equals value minus mortgage balance, so $250,000 minus $180,000 is $70,000, which is the share of the home the owner holds.

ww.$180,000: $180,000 is the mortgage balance still owed, which is subtracted from the home value, not the amount of equity.
ww.$250,000: $250,000 is the market value of the home, and equity requires subtracting the $180,000 owed, so this ignores the loan.
ww.$430,000: $430,000 comes from adding the value and the loan, but equity is found by subtracting the mortgage balance from the value.

rw: Closing costs are fees paid when a real estate purchase is completed, including lender charges, title insurance, appraisal and recording fees.

ww.The home price agreed upon by the buyer: The agreed home price is the purchase price, which is separate from closing costs, the extra fees paid at completion of the sale.
ww.The down payment made by the buyer to th: The down payment is part of the purchase price paid upfront, while closing costs are additional fees for services such as title and appraisal.
ww.Monthly rent paid by the tenant to the l: Monthly rent from tenant to landlord is an ongoing housing cost, while closing costs are one-time fees at the end of a purchase.

rw: Under 50/30/20, savings and debt repayment get 20 percent, and 20 percent of $2,500 is 0.20 times 2,500, which equals $500.

ww.$750: $750 is 30 percent of $2,500, which is the wants share of the guideline, not the savings and debt repayment share.
ww.$1,250: $1,250 is 50 percent of $2,500, which is the needs share of the guideline, not the savings and debt repayment share.
ww.$250: $250 is only 10 percent of $2,500, which is half of the 20 percent that the guideline assigns to savings and debt.

rw: Needs total $1,400 plus $500 plus $300, which is $2,200, and $2,200 divided by $3,500 is about 0.63, or 63 percent of income.

ww.Is 40 percent: Forty percent would be about $1,400 divided by $3,500, which counts only rent and leaves out the food and utilities in the total.
ww.Is 37 percent: Thirty-seven percent is what is left over, 100 minus 63, so it is the share of income not spent on these needs.
ww.Is 100 percent: One hundred percent would mean needs use all of the $3,500, but $2,200 is only about 63 percent of that income.

rw: Variance is actual minus budget, so $72 minus $60 equals $12, and since spending exceeded the plan, it is over budget.

ww.$12 under budget: Spending $72 against a $60 budget is more than planned, so the variance is over budget and not under budget as stated.
ww.$132 over budget: $132 adds the budget and the spending together, but variance is the difference between them, which is $72 minus $60, or $12.
ww.$6 over budget: $6 is half of the real difference, and subtracting $60 from $72 gives $12, not $6.

rw: Income comes first because every spending and saving amount in a budget depends on how much money is available to allocate.

ww.Gifts: Gifts are a variable, optional spending category that is planned only after income is known, so it should not be recorded first.
ww.Dining: Dining out is a discretionary expense that depends on how much income is available, so it is not the first line.
ww.Concerts: Concerts are an optional entertainment cost, planned only after income and necessities are known, so they are not recorded first.

rw: Budgeting apps connect to accounts and categorize transactions automatically, which shows where money goes and helps people stay within their plan.

ww.To remove the need to check any bank sta: A budgeting app does not remove the need to check bank statements, since statements are still needed to verify transactions and catch errors.
ww.To increase income automatically without: An app tracks money but cannot raise pay automatically, because income only grows through work, raises or other earnings.
ww.To guarantee that spending will never ex: No app can guarantee that spending stays under income, because the user still decides what to buy and when to stop.

rw: Money left after fixed expenses is $900 minus $600, which equals $300 available for variable spending and savings each month.

ww.$150: $150 is half of the real remainder, and subtracting the $600 of fixed expenses from $900 gives $300 instead.
ww.$1,500: $1,500 adds the income and the fixed expenses together, but what is left over requires subtracting expenses from income.
ww.$600: $600 is the amount of fixed expenses themselves, not the remainder, which is $900 minus $600, or $300.

rw: A sinking fund spreads an annual bill over monthly deposits, so for a $600 bill saving $50 a month covers it when due.

ww.Borrow from a friend on the day that the: Borrowing from a friend on the due date creates a debt and strain on a relationship when the bill could be planned for.
ww.Ignore it until the bill arrives, then u: Ignoring the bill until it arrives and then using a card adds interest and debt, when saving ahead would avoid it.
ww.Skip the bill and hope that no one will: Skipping the bill risks penalties, fines or loss of registration, and someone is certain to notice, so it is not a sound plan.

rw: A cash-flow statement tracks inflows and outflows of money over a period, showing whether the household takes in more than it spends.

ww.A document that shows the value of the f: The value of the family home belongs on a balance sheet or appraisal, not in a statement tracking money moving in and out.
ww.A forecast of the prices of goods in sho: A forecast of shop prices is an economic projection, whereas a household cash-flow statement records the family's own income and spending over time.
ww.A list of everything the household owns: A list of everything owned and owed on one date is a net worth or balance sheet statement, not a cash-flow statement.

rw: Savings are $4,000 minus $3,200, or $800, and $800 divided by $4,000 equals 0.20, so the household saves 20 percent of income.

ww.8 percent: Eight percent would come from a savings of $320, but savings here are $800, which is a larger share of income.
ww.80 percent: Eighty percent is the share of income that goes to expenses, $3,200 divided by $4,000, not the share that is saved.
ww.25 percent: Twenty-five percent comes from dividing $800 by $3,200, the expenses, but the savings rate divides by income, which is $4,000.

rw: Spending that repeatedly exceeds income means the plan is unrealistic or too loose, so categories or amounts need to be changed.

ww.Bills are paid before the due date: Paying bills early shows the budget is working well, so it gives no reason to change the plan.
ww.Income matches what was expected: When income matches expectations, the budget's assumptions hold true and the plan does not need revising.
ww.Savings goals are being met on time: Meeting savings goals on time shows the budget is succeeding, so there is no reason to change it.

rw: A windfall is an unexpected sum of money, like a bonus, tax refund, gift or inheritance, that was not part of regular income.

ww.A loan received from a bank at a low rat: A bank loan at a low rate is borrowed money that must be repaid, whereas a windfall is unexpected money you receive.
ww.A regular payment received each month fr: A regular monthly payment from an employer is a paycheck, which is expected, so it is not an unexpected windfall.
ww.A bill that arrives once a year, such as: A yearly bill such as property tax is an expense that can be planned in advance, not unexpected money that arrives.

rw: Paying down the card gives a guaranteed return equal to the 22 percent interest avoided, which beats nearly any savings account or investment.

ww.Put it in a plain savings account: A plain savings account pays far less than the 22 percent charged on the card debt, so the debt costs far more than savings earn.
ww.Lend it to a friend to repay later: Lending to a friend risks never being repaid and earns nothing, while the credit card debt keeps charging 22 percent interest.
ww.Spend all of it on a vacation trip: Spending it all on a vacation adds nothing to financial health, and the 22 percent card interest would keep growing on the balance.

rw: Gross weekly pay is hourly rate times hours, so $18 times 30 equals $540 before any taxes or deductions are taken out.

ww.$600: $600 would be about $20 an hour times 30 hours, but the wage is $18 an hour, not $20.
ww.$1.67: $1.67 comes from dividing 30 by 18, but pay is found by multiplying the hourly wage by the hours worked.
ww.$48: $48 comes from adding $18 and 30 hours, but wages are multiplied by hours, so adding the two numbers is meaningless.

rw: Time-and-a-half means 1.5 times the regular wage, so $15 times 1.5 equals $22.50 for each overtime hour worked.

ww.$15: $15 is just the regular hourly wage, and overtime at time-and-a-half must pay more than the normal rate.
ww.$16.50: $16.50 adds only 10 percent to the wage, but time-and-a-half adds 50 percent, which is $7.50 on $15.
ww.$30: $30 is double time, two times the $15 wage, whereas time-and-a-half is 1.5 times the wage, or $22.50.

rw: A routing number is a nine-digit code that identifies the bank or credit union holding the account so payments are routed correctly.

ww.The date the account was opened by the o: The date an account was opened is recorded in bank files, but it has no role in the routing number.
ww.The individual account of the bank's cus: The individual customer account is identified by the account number, while the routing number is shared by all of a bank's accounts.
ww.The branch manager who approved the acco: A routing number does not identify a manager or any person, only the financial institution where the account is held.

rw: Adjusted balance equals $1,200 minus $150 in outstanding checks plus $100 deposit in transit, which gives $1,150 after both adjustments.

ww.$1,300: $1,300 adds the deposit but also adds back the checks instead of subtracting them, and neither treatment is correct.
ww.$1,450: $1,450 adds both the $150 in checks and the $100 deposit to the balance, but outstanding checks must be subtracted.
ww.$1,050: $1,050 subtracts the $150 in checks and then also subtracts the $100 deposit, but a deposit in transit must be added.

rw: Standard checking accounts are built for everyday spending and typically pay little or no interest, so they pay the least.

ww.A money market type account: Money market accounts usually pay more than checking, because they hold larger balances and earn better rates than basic accounts.
ww.A five-year CD at a bank: A five-year CD locks money in for a long term and normally pays one of the higher rates among bank products.
ww.A high-yield savings account: High-yield savings accounts are designed to pay rates well above standard accounts, so they pay far more than checking.

rw: A joint account is owned by two or more people, who can each deposit and withdraw, such as spouses or partners.

ww.An account only for the bank's own staff: An account for bank staff only is an employee account, but a joint account is shared between customers of the bank.
ww.An account shared by a bank with the sta: A bank does not share an account with the state, and a joint account is held by customers who share ownership.
ww.An account open only to young children: Joint accounts are open to adults and are not limited to young children, who usually need an adult co-owner anyway.

rw: An EFT moves money between accounts electronically, as with direct deposit, online bill pay or ACH transfers, without paper checks or cash.

ww.A coin deposit made at a machine in a sh: Depositing coins at a machine in a shop is a physical cash deposit, not an electronic movement of funds between accounts.
ww.A paper check mailed to a payee for depo: A paper check is a physical instrument, which is the older method that electronic transfers replaced, so it is not an EFT.
ww.A cash deposit made in person at a branc: A cash deposit made in person is physical money handed to a teller, which is not an electronic transfer of funds.

rw: Reporting a lost debit card right away lets the bank block it and limits your liability for any unauthorized charges.

ww.Post the card number on social media: Posting the card number on social media would let thieves use it, so it exposes you to fraud instead of protecting you.
ww.Wait weeks before telling the bank: Waiting weeks lets thieves keep spending, and delaying the report can raise your liability from $50 to $500 or more.
ww.Tell no one and hope no one finds it: Telling no one and hoping lets anyone who finds the card drain your account, so you lose protection by doing nothing.

rw: Reporting within two business days limits liability to $50 under the Electronic Fund Transfer Act, while later reports can cost much more.

ww.Within one year of loss: One year is far too late, since waiting beyond 60 days after the statement can leave you liable for all losses.
ww.Never, as the bank pays all: The bank does not pay everything automatically, since your liability depends on how quickly you report, so waiting indefinitely offers no protection.
ww.Within thirty days of loss: Reporting within thirty days raises liability to as much as $500, so only a report inside two business days holds it to $50.

rw: A service charge is a fee a bank imposes for maintaining an account or for services like wire transfers, overdrafts and paper statements.

ww.Interest paid by the bank on the balance: Interest paid by the bank on a balance is earnings for the customer, while a service charge is a cost charged to the customer.
ww.A tax collected by the government on ban: A government tax on deposits is not a service charge, which is a fee the bank itself sets for its services.
ww.A reward for opening an account, such as: A reward for opening an account is a bonus or promotion paid to the customer, which is the reverse of a charge.

rw: Many accounts waive monthly fees if you keep a required minimum balance, so meeting it is the surest way to avoid them.

ww.Closing and reopening the account every: Closing and reopening the account each month adds paperwork and can trigger new fees, and it does nothing to waive monthly charges.
ww.Making many small withdrawals to keep th: Making many small withdrawals keeps the balance low, which is the very thing that triggers monthly fees on accounts with a minimum.
ww.Overdrawing the account so the bank sees: Overdrawing the account causes overdraft fees and negative balances, which add charges rather than avoiding monthly account fees.

rw: A custodial account is managed by an adult, the custodian, for the benefit of a minor until the child reaches the age of majority.

ww.An account for businesses only, managed: A business-only account managed by the owner is a commercial account, while a custodial account is held for a minor.
ww.An account the government opens for ever: Governments do not open custodial accounts for citizens, because these accounts are set up by an adult for a child.
ww.An account that is managed by a bank for: Accounts managed by a bank for its own staff are internal accounts, not custodial accounts, which exist to benefit minors.

rw: A high-yield savings account pays a higher interest rate than a standard savings account, so balances grow faster with the same deposit.

ww.A savings account that charges a fee eac: Charging a fee for each deposit would make an account worse, whereas a high-yield savings account offers a better interest rate.
ww.A savings account that pays no interest: Paying no interest contradicts the name, since high-yield accounts exist to pay more interest, and free checks are not the point.
ww.A savings account that can be opened onl: High-yield accounts commonly have low or no minimums, so requiring a very large deposit is not part of the definition.

rw: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time, so $1,200 times 0.03 times 2 gives $72 earned over the two years.

ww.$36: $36 is the interest for only one year, $1,200 times 0.03, and the question asks for two years, which doubles it.
ww.$1,272: $1,272 is the total balance at the end, principal plus the $72 of interest, and the question asks only for the interest.
ww.$720: $720 comes from using 30 percent rather than 3 percent, which puts the decimal point in the wrong place by one digit.

rw: Utilization equals balance divided by limit, so $2,000 divided by $8,000 is 0.25, or 25 percent of available credit used.

ww.10 percent: Ten percent would need a balance of $800, but the balance here is $2,000, which is a bigger share of the $8,000 limit.
ww.400 percent: Four hundred percent flips the fraction, $8,000 divided by $2,000, but utilization is the balance divided by the limit.
ww.75 percent: Seventy-five percent is the unused credit, $6,000 of $8,000, but utilization measures the share that is used, not the share left.

rw: On-time payments are the biggest factor in a score, and keeping balances low lowers utilization, so both habits raise a score over time.

ww.Opening many new credit cards in a short: Opening many cards quickly creates several hard inquiries and lowers average account age, which usually hurts a score in the short term.
ww.Maxing out cards each month and paying o: Maxing out cards pushes utilization very high, and paying only the minimum keeps balances high, both of which lower a score.
ww.Closing the oldest account to shorten hi: Closing the oldest account shortens credit history and lowers available credit, which tends to reduce a score instead of raising it.

rw: A credit report records a person's borrowing and repayment history, including accounts, balances, payment record and inquiries, as compiled by credit bureaus.

ww.A list of grocery purchases kept in a ho: Grocery purchases kept in a household notebook are personal records, whereas a credit report is compiled by credit bureaus about borrowing.
ww.A statement of the balance of a person's: A savings balance statement comes from your bank, and it is not part of what a credit report records about debts.
ww.A document that shows how much a person: Income is not listed on a credit report, which is about borrowing history and not about how much a person earns.

rw: A credit limit is the maximum amount the lender lets you borrow on a card, and going over it can bring fees.

ww.The number of cards you are allowed to h: The number of cards you hold is not the limit; a credit limit is the dollar amount available on a single card.
ww.The total interest that you will pay ove: Total interest over the life of a card is a cost that varies with balances and time, not a limit set by the lender.
ww.The minimum payment you must make each m: The minimum payment is the smallest amount due each month, which is a separate figure from the credit limit.

rw: Monthly interest is 24 percent divided by 12, or 2 percent, and 2 percent of $1,000 is about $20 each month.

ww.About $240: $240 is the interest for a full year at 24 percent on $1,000, not for one month, so it is twelve times too high.
ww.About $200: $200 would come from 20 percent a month, but 24 percent APR divided by 12 months is 2 percent a month.
ww.About $2: $2 would be 0.2 percent of $1,000, which misplaces the decimal, since 2 percent of $1,000 is $20.

rw: A charge-off is when a lender gives up on collecting and writes the debt off as a loss, though the borrower still owes it.

ww.When a borrower is given extra time to r: Extra time to repay with no penalty is a forbearance or grace arrangement, not a charge-off, which is a lender's accounting loss.
ww.When a lender raises the credit limit of: Raising the credit limit of a good customer is an upgrade, and it has nothing to do with a debt written off.
ww.When a borrower pays off a debt early an: Paying a debt off early closes the account in good standing, whereas a charge-off happens when the borrower has not paid.

rw: A collection account is a past-due debt that the original lender has turned over to a collector, and it harms credit.

ww.A list of coins that a person has gather: A hobby coin collection has nothing to do with credit, and a collection account is a debt, not a set of coins.
ww.A savings account banks use to collect s: Banks do not use savings to collect small deposits as collection accounts, which are overdue debts in the hands of collectors.
ww.A credit card account with a low interes: A low-rate card with no fee is a favorable product, while a collection account signals unpaid debt and damages credit.

rw: The Fair Debt Collection Practices Act bans abusive, deceptive and harassing collection tactics such as threats, false statements and repeated calls at unreasonable hours.

ww.Charging interest on any loan made to a: The Act does not ban interest on loans, because lenders may legally charge interest, and it governs how collectors behave.
ww.Reporting debts to the credit bureaus ev: Reporting debts to credit bureaus is lawful and common, and the Act does not forbid creditors from doing it.
ww.Opening a savings account at a bank with: Opening a savings account is ordinary banking and unrelated to debt collection, which is the only thing the Act regulates.

rw: Calling at midnight and threatening arrest breaks the Fair Debt Collection Practices Act, since collectors may not call at odd hours or make false threats.

ww.A requirement of the card contract allow: Card contracts cannot override federal law, so no agreement can allow harassing night calls or arrest threats by a collector.
ww.A normal collection step that debt colle: Debt collectors must follow the law, and calling at midnight with threats of arrest is not a normal or permitted step.
ww.A courtesy reminder that the law itself: The law does not encourage this behavior; it prohibits threats and calls at unreasonable hours, so it cannot be a courtesy reminder.

rw: The Truth in Lending Act requires lenders to disclose the cost of credit, including the APR, finance charges and the total of payments.

ww.The salary of each of the lender's emplo: Employee salaries are private business information, and lenders are not required to disclose them under the Truth in Lending Act.
ww.The names of the lender's largest compet: Competitors' names are marketing information, and the Act does not require lenders to disclose them to borrowers.
ww.The home addresses of every other borrow: Other borrowers' addresses are private data that lenders must protect, so disclosing them would violate privacy and not the Act's purpose.

rw: A finance charge is the total cost of borrowing, including interest and fees like origination or service charges, which the borrower pays.

ww.The amount a borrower repays as principa: Principal is the amount borrowed and repaid, but a finance charge is the added cost of borrowing, not the principal itself.
ww.The monthly rent a borrower pays for a h: Monthly rent for a home is a housing cost and has no link to the cost of borrowing money.
ww.The tax a borrower pays to the state for: A finance charge is paid to the lender as part of the credit cost, rather than a tax paid to the state.

rw: A penalty APR is a higher interest rate that the card issuer may apply after a late or missed payment, per the card terms.

ww.A bonus rate that applies to new cardhol: A bonus rate for new cardholders is an introductory or promotional APR, which is low, while a penalty APR is high.
ww.A fee that is charged for using the card: A fee for using the card abroad is a foreign transaction fee, which is a flat charge and not an interest rate.
ww.A lower rate given to customers who pay: A penalty APR raises the rate after misbehavior, so a lower rate for early payers is the reverse of what it does.

rw: An introductory 0 percent APR is a temporary low rate offered when you open a card, and it ends after months.

ww.A permanent rate that never changes in t: An introductory rate is temporary, ending after a set period, so calling it permanent and unchanging for the card's life is wrong.
ww.A rate that is charged on purchases made: A rate on purchases abroad is not an introductory rate, because foreign charges usually bring fees and the offer applies to the card generally.
ww.A rate that applies only to cash advance: Cash advance rates are usually higher and are not introductory, since the offer typically applies to purchases or balance transfers instead.

rw: Paying the balance before the 0 percent period ends avoids the 22 percent rate, so you borrow for free and avoid interest.

ww.Spend as much as possible in the promoti: Spending as much as possible builds a large balance that will start costing 22 percent interest once the promotion ends.
ww.Ignore the date when the rate will chang: The rate change is significant, because a balance left after 12 months will begin accruing 22 percent interest, so the date matters.
ww.Close the account on the last day withou: Closing the account without paying leaves the debt unpaid, which invites late fees, collections and damage to the credit score.

rw: A co-borrower applies with the main borrower and shares equal legal responsibility for repaying the loan from the start.

ww.A person who repays a loan only if the m: A person who pays only if the main borrower fails is a co-signer, whereas a co-borrower shares responsibility from the beginning.
ww.A person who approves a loan for a bank: Approving a loan on behalf of a bank is the job of a loan officer or underwriter, not a co-borrower.
ww.A person who lends money to a borrower w: A person who lends money to a borrower without interest is a lender or a generous friend, not a co-borrower on a loan.

rw: Deferment pauses payments, for example while in school or unemployed, and on some federal loans interest does not build up during the pause.

ww.A penalty charged to students who miss a: A penalty for missing a payment is a late fee, which is unrelated to deferment, a pause in payments.
ww.A permanent cancellation of the whole lo: Deferment does not cancel a loan, so the borrower must still repay it later, and cancellation is called discharge or forgiveness.
ww.A higher interest rate for borrowers who: Deferment has nothing to do with studying abroad or a higher interest rate, because it is a pause granted for eligible situations.

rw: Federal loans have terms and protections set by the government, such as income-driven repayment and deferment, while private loans come from banks with lender-set terms.

ww.Federal loans must be repaid in full wit: Federal loans have long repayment terms, often ten years or more, and are not due in full one year after graduation.
ww.Private loans are always forgiven after: Private loans are not forgiven after ten years, because forgiveness programs exist mainly for federal loans with specific requirements.
ww.Private loans always have lower interest: Private loans often charge higher rates than federal loans, and they do not allow the same repayment plans, so this is false.

rw: Simple interest equals principal times rate times time, so $10,000 times 0.05 times 4 gives $2,000 of total interest.

ww.$500: $500 is the simple interest for only one year, $10,000 times 0.05, and the loan runs for four years.
ww.$12,000: $12,000 is the principal plus the $2,000 of interest, which is the total repaid, and the question asks only for interest.
ww.$20,000: $20,000 does not follow from any step, because multiplying $10,000 by 5 percent for 4 years gives only $2,000 in interest.

rw: Amortization pays off a loan through regular payments that cover interest and principal, so the balance falls to zero by the end.

ww.Paying the loan off in one lump sum on t: A lump-sum payment on day one is a single payoff, whereas amortization spreads payments over the life of the loan.
ww.Paying only the interest on a loan for y: Paying only interest and never reducing principal is an interest-only loan, while amortization gradually reduces the principal balance too.
ww.Canceling the loan when the borrower ask: Canceling a loan on request is simply early termination, which is a different matter from the scheduled repayment that amortization describes.

rw: A longer term stretches the principal over more months so the payments are smaller, but interest accrues longer and totals more.

ww.Zero interest, since time reduces the bo: A longer term does not make interest zero, since interest accrues for more months, which usually raises the total cost.
ww.Higher monthly payments and less total i: A longer term spreads payments out, which lowers each monthly payment, so claiming higher payments with less interest is backwards.
ww.The same total interest as a shorter loa: Total interest depends on the time the balance is outstanding, so a longer term costs more in interest than a short one.

rw: The 3-year loan has a higher payment but pays interest for fewer months, so the total interest cost is lower than with 5 years.

ww.It leaves a higher final balance: A shorter loan pays down principal faster, so the final balance is lower, which makes a higher final balance wrong.
ww.It has a lower rate every time: The rate is the same 6 percent in both cases, so the 3-year loan does not carry a lower rate, and the savings come from time.
ww.It avoids paying any interest: Both loans charge 6 percent interest, so neither avoids interest, though the shorter term pays much less of it.

rw: The Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act governs written warranties on consumer products, requiring clear disclosure of terms and giving buyers remedies when companies fail to honor them.

ww.Employment contracts on pay and hours: Employment contracts on pay and hours fall under labor laws such as the Fair Labor Standards Act, not the Magnuson-Moss Act.
ww.The interest rates banks charge on car l: Interest rates on car loans are covered by lending laws like the Truth in Lending Act, not the Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act.
ww.The prices of goods in retail stores: The Act does not control retail prices, which businesses set themselves, and it applies to warranty terms on products instead.

rw: A lemon law is a state law that protects buyers of new vehicles with serious defects the maker cannot repair, offering a refund or replacement.

ww.A law that bans the sale of fruit in sto: Lemon laws are about defective vehicles, not fruit, so a ban on selling fruit in stores has no connection to the name.
ww.A law that taxes the sale of used cars a: Lemon laws do not tax used car sales; they give remedies for defective vehicles, and a sales tax is a different matter.
ww.A law on car insurance setting minimum c: Minimum car insurance coverage is set by separate state financial responsibility laws, not by lemon laws about defective vehicles.

rw: The FTC rule lets buyers cancel certain door-to-door and similar sales within three days, and the seller must tell them of this right.

ww.Buyers can cancel any purchase within a: The Cooling-Off Rule gives three days and not a year, and it applies only to certain sales, not to any purchase.
ww.Sellers can cancel at any time, whatever: The rule protects buyers, not sellers, and sellers cannot cancel at any time regardless of what was promised.
ww.Buyers must wait three days before they: The rule gives buyers three days to cancel, rather than forcing them to wait before using the product.

rw: Bait-and-switch advertises a low-priced item to attract customers and then pressures them into buying a more expensive one, which is deceptive and illegal.

ww.Giving customers a free sample before th: Giving a free sample is a legal promotion, whereas bait-and-switch is a deceptive tactic that advertises one item and pushes another.
ww.Switching to a new brand name openly wit: Openly switching a brand name with a posted notice is honest, while bait-and-switch relies on deception about the item offered.
ww.Lowering the price of an item during a s: Lowering a price for everyone during a sale is a genuine discount, not a trick that lures customers with an item unavailable.

rw: Truth in advertising requires ads to be truthful and not misleading, backed by evidence for claims, as enforced by the FTC.

ww.Ads must be written in small print: Truth in advertising does not require small print, and burying key terms in small print can make an ad misleading.
ww.Ads must show only the lowest price: Ads need not show only the lowest price, since the rule is about honesty, not about displaying any particular price.
ww.Ads must be approved by each buyer first: Ads need no approval from each buyer, because the rule sets honesty standards that apply to advertisers without individual consent.

rw: Real prizes never require upfront fees, so hanging up is the right response to a caller asking for payment first.

ww.Pay the fee by gift card to claim the pr: Gift cards are untraceable and favored by scammers, so paying a fee that way would only lose money with no prize.
ww.Give your bank details, so the prize can: Giving bank details to an unknown caller lets scammers drain the account, and a real prize needs no such information.
ww.Send a copy of your ID by email to the c: Emailing a copy of your ID invites identity theft, and a legitimate prize never requires a stranger to receive your ID.

rw: A gift card scam is a demand to pay with gift cards, which are hard to trace or recover, so no real agency does this.

ww.A form of savings account offered by ban: A savings account is a bank deposit product, but a gift card scam is a fraud, not any form of savings.
ww.A way for stores to give discounts to lo: Store discounts for loyal customers are legitimate marketing, which is the reverse of a fraud that demands payment by gift card.
ww.A required payment method for bills, acc: Utilities and government bodies do not require payment by gift card, so presenting it as required is itself a hallmark of the scam.

rw: Trusted sites, reviews and a credit card together protect you, since cards offer dispute rights and fraud limits that other methods lack.

ww.Click links in unsolicited emails offeri: Clicking links in unsolicited emails is a common way to land on fake sites, so deep-discount offers should be avoided.
ww.Pay by wire transfer to a seller you hav: Wire transfers are nearly impossible to reverse, so paying a stranger by wire leaves you no recourse if the seller is fake.
ww.Share your password with the seller to s: Passwords should never be shared with a seller, and doing so gives a scammer access to your accounts and money.

rw: A hidden fee is a charge not clearly disclosed up front, such as a surprise service or processing fee added at checkout.

ww.A tax shown on the receipt at the bottom: A tax shown on the receipt is disclosed openly, so it is not hidden, and it is a different kind of charge.
ww.A bonus given to customers for large buy: A bonus given to customers is a benefit, whereas a hidden fee is a cost the customer pays unexpectedly.
ww.A discount a store applies at the regist: A discount applied at the register lowers the price, so it benefits the customer and is the opposite of a fee.

rw: A subscription trap is a free trial that quietly converts to a paid plan unless you cancel in time, often with hard cancellation.

ww.A free product that comes with every pai: A free product with every plan and no terms would not trap anyone, since a subscription trap involves charges that begin without clear warning.
ww.A refund that is paid automatically each: A refund paid automatically each month would favor the customer, whereas a trap costs the customer money by charging them repeatedly.
ww.A discount that never ends for customers: A permanent discount for loyal customers is a benefit, not a trap, which depends on hidden recurring charges instead.

rw: The warranty is the document that states what the maker will repair or replace, how long coverage lasts and any conditions.

ww.The receipt: A receipt proves the purchase and its date, but it does not usually list the repair or replacement terms for defects.
ww.The ad copy: Ad copy makes promotional claims, but it is not the binding document that states repair or replacement terms after purchase.
ww.The shopping bag: A shopping bag is only packaging and holds no terms, so it cannot state repair or replacement terms for the phone.

rw: A return policy is the store's own rule about returns for refund or exchange, including time limits and the condition of items.

ww.A law forcing stores to refund all purch: No law forces stores to refund every purchase, because return policies are set by stores except where specific laws apply.
ww.A product's warranty only, covering repa: A warranty covers repairs for defects, whereas a return policy covers sending items back for a refund or exchange.
ww.A rule that customers must follow when t: Rules customers follow while shopping are store conduct policies, whereas a return policy deals specifically with returning purchased items afterward.

rw: Contacting the card issuer to dispute the charge quickly starts the investigation and limits your liability under federal protections for unauthorized use.

ww.Ignore it, since small charges are not w: Ignoring an unauthorized charge lets it stand and can let fraud continue, and disputes must be made within time limits.
ww.Pay it to avoid trouble, then ask the st: Paying an unauthorized charge can be taken as acceptance and wastes money, when you can dispute it with the issuer instead.
ww.Post about it on social media and wait f: Posting on social media does not notify the issuer, which is the party able to reverse the charge and protect you.

rw: The Fair Credit Billing Act limits a cardholder's liability for unauthorized credit card charges to $50 and sets a dispute process.

ww.The Sherman Act of 1890: The Sherman Act of 1890 deals with monopolies and competition between firms, and it has nothing to do with cardholder liability.
ww.The Clean Air Act of 1970: The Clean Air Act of 1970 regulates pollution, and it does not address credit card liability in any way.
ww.The Fair Labor Standards Act: The Fair Labor Standards Act sets minimum wage and overtime rules for workers, so it does not cover unauthorized card use.

rw: A chargeback reverses a card payment after the cardholder disputes it, returning funds from the merchant when there was fraud or a billing error.

ww.A tax collected on goods that a customer: A tax collected on goods bought abroad is a customs duty, whereas a chargeback is a reversal of a card payment.
ww.A bonus that a store gives to a customer: A bonus for paying with cash is a cash discount, which differs from a chargeback, a reversal of a disputed card payment.
ww.A fee that a store charges a customer fo: A fee charged for paying by credit card is a surcharge, which is paid to the store, whereas a chargeback returns money.

rw: A credit freeze blocks lenders from viewing your credit file, which prevents new accounts from being opened in your name by thieves.

ww.A freeze on the interest rate of the loa: A freeze does not lock an interest rate, since rate locks are a loan feature and a freeze concerns access to your credit file.
ww.A ban on all credit use forever after on: A freeze is not a punishment for one late payment, and you control it, lifting it whenever you want to apply for credit.
ww.A fee for freezing assets, charged by th: A credit freeze is typically free by law, not a fee for freezing assets, and it concerns your credit file instead of bank assets.

rw: A fraud alert tells lenders to verify your identity before granting credit, which helps stop thieves from opening accounts in your name.

ww.A ban on all credit use forever after on: A permanent ban on credit use after one late payment does not exist, and a fraud alert is a short-term notice on your file.
ww.A bonus offered to customers who report: A fraud alert is not a reward and costs nothing, and it is placed by the consumer, not paid by the lender.
ww.A message sent to your phone each time t: A message to your phone after each purchase is a transaction alert from the card issuer, not a fraud alert on a credit file.

rw: A fraud alert or freeze blocks new credit in your name, and monitoring accounts helps you catch any misuse quickly.

ww.Close your bank accounts at random so th: Closing accounts at random does not stop thieves who already hold your data, and it can hurt your credit history and score.
ww.Do nothing, since the breach affects onl: Doing nothing leaves your personal data exposed, and a breach can lead to identity theft that harms you directly.
ww.Share your passwords with friends so the: Sharing passwords gives others access to your accounts and creates a new risk, so it cannot protect your credit.

rw: Phishing emails create urgency and include a link that asks for your password, so they can steal your credentials.

ww.A message from your bank that asks for n: A message from a bank that asks for no personal data is consistent with real bank behavior, so it is not a warning sign.
ww.A message that has no links and only giv: A message with only information and no links gives the scammer no way to steal credentials, so it does not look like phishing.
ww.A message from a known contact about a c: A message from a known contact about a chat you actually had is consistent with normal communication, so it is not suspicious.

rw: A fireproof box or safe protects important documents from fire, theft and loss, and it is the right place for them.

ww.In the glove compartment of your parked: A glove compartment can be stolen, damaged by heat and broken into, so it is a poor place for a birth certificate.
ww.In your wallet each day so you have it f: Carrying a birth certificate in your wallet every day risks losing it or having it stolen, which invites identity theft.
ww.In an envelope on your desk at work all: An envelope on a desk at work is unsecured and visible to others, and it offers no protection from fire or theft.

rw: Four years is 48 months, and $12,000 divided by 48 equals $250 a month, which reaches the goal ignoring interest.

ww.$48: $48 is four years of months, 4 times 12, and not a monthly savings amount, so it divides by the wrong quantity.
ww.$3,000: $3,000 per month would be far too much; $12,000 divided by 4 gives $3,000 per year, and the question asks about months.
ww.$1,000: $1,000 a month would reach $12,000 in just 12 months, one year, rather than the 4 years the family has.

rw: Saving for retirement 35 years away is a long-term goal, because it takes many years of planning, contributions and growth.

ww.Paying for lunch this week only: Paying for lunch this week is a short-term goal because it is needed right away, so it is not a long-term one.
ww.Buying a pair of shoes at the weekend: Buying shoes at the weekend is an immediate purchase, so it falls in the short-term category and not the long term.
ww.Setting aside money for a phone bill: Setting aside money for a phone bill is a short-term goal since the bill comes due within weeks or a month.

rw: Defining the goal, the amount and the date makes it specific and measurable, which lets you plan how much to save.

ww.Choose a goal that is as large as can be: Choosing the largest possible goal ignores what is realistic, and a goal should be achievable, not simply as large as can be.
ww.Wait for money to be left at month end: Waiting for leftover money means saving never starts, since without a plan the money tends to be spent elsewhere.
ww.Spend first and decide the goal later: Spending first and choosing a goal later leaves nothing for the goal, because the money is already gone by then.

rw: Prioritizing means ranking goals by importance and urgency so the most important ones get funded first when money is limited.

ww.Save for all goals equally with no order: Saving equally for every goal with no order ignores that some goals are more urgent or important, so it is not prioritizing.
ww.Choose the cheapest goal and drop others: Choosing the cheapest goal and dropping the others ignores what matters most, so it is not a ranking by importance.
ww.Ignore goals that take over a year: Ignoring goals that take over a year would drop long-term goals like retirement, which are often important and need early planning.

rw: Dividing the $1,800 price by 9 months gives $200 per month, which reaches the laptop price exactly at the end.

ww.$16,200: $16,200 multiplies 1,800 by 9 instead of dividing, which gives a number far larger than the price of the laptop.
ww.$900: $900 is half of the price, which would reach the goal in 2 months, not the 9 months the person has.
ww.$162: $162 does not come from dividing $1,800 by 9 months, which equals $200, so it falls short and would leave the goal underfunded.

rw: Needs, income and time horizons change with life stage, so young people may save for a home or degree while retirees plan withdrawals.

ww.Retirees always have a higher income tha: Retirees do not always earn more than young workers, since many live on fixed pensions or savings, so this claim is false.
ww.Young people need no savings, and retire: Young people do need savings and retirees do need insurance, such as health coverage, so both halves of this claim are wrong.
ww.Goals do not change as people age or mov: Goals do change with age, because circumstances, responsibilities and income differ from youth to retirement, so this is false.

rw: A financial plan is a roadmap for reaching money goals, using income, savings, spending and investing decisions over time.

ww.A bank statement that shows the balance: A bank statement is a record of past transactions and balance, whereas a financial plan looks ahead to reach goals.
ww.A single bill that must be paid by the f: A single bill is just one payment obligation, while a financial plan covers goals and how income, saving and spending fit together.
ww.A list of items to buy at the store, wit: A shopping list covers items to buy, whereas a financial plan covers long-term goals and the steps to fund them.

rw: A 529 plan is a tax-advantaged account for saving for education costs, with earnings that can grow tax-free when used for school.

ww.Paying for a vacation trip abroad this s: A vacation is not a qualified education expense, so a 529 plan is not meant for paying for a trip.
ww.Saving for retirement at age 65, many ye: Retirement savings go in accounts like a 401(k) or IRA, while a 529 plan is designed for education costs.
ww.Paying off credit card bills each month: Paying off credit card bills is not what a 529 does, since withdrawals for non-education uses can bring taxes and penalties.

rw: Five years is 60 months, so $150 times 60 equals $9,000, and with no interest earned the total is only the deposits.

ww.$750: $750 is 150 times 5, which treats the five years as five months, and a year has twelve months of saving.
ww.$900: $900 is 150 times 6, only six months of saving, while five years contains many more months of deposits.
ww.$1,800: $1,800 is 150 times 12, which is just one year of saving, but the person saves for five years.

rw: Saving early gives more years for compounding, so earnings themselves earn returns and the account can grow much larger by retirement.

ww.Banks pay younger savers a higher fixed: Banks do not give younger savers a higher fixed rate because of age, since rates depend on the product and market conditions.
ww.Early savers never pay any fees on funds: Fees can apply to any account regardless of when you start saving, so early savers are not exempt from them.
ww.Taxes disappear for early savers on all: Taxes do not vanish for early savers, though some accounts are tax-advantaged, and the benefit is not tied to starting early.

rw: Financial responsibility means managing money wisely, such as budgeting, saving and avoiding excess debt, and meeting your obligations on time.

ww.Spending whatever you wish and paying bi: Spending whatever you wish and paying bills only at times shows a lack of responsibility, since obligations should be met consistently.
ww.Avoiding all records of your income and: Avoiding records of income and spending makes it hard to budget or file taxes, which is the opposite of being responsible.
ww.Borrowing as much as possible from every: Borrowing as much as possible from every lender leads to unmanageable debt, so it is reckless and not responsible.

rw: Reminders or automatic payments make sure bills are paid by the due date, which avoids late fees and credit damage.

ww.Pay only the bills over 30 days late: Paying only bills that are over 30 days late already means penalties and credit report damage have happened, so it is a bad habit.
ww.Pay bills in the order you find them: Paying bills in the order you find them ignores due dates, so a bill due soon may be missed and charged a fee.
ww.Wait until a collector calls to pay a bi: Waiting for a collector to call means the bill is badly overdue, which damages credit and adds fees, and is a poor habit.

rw: Automatic payment or reminders a few days early ensure the bill is paid on time even when you are busy.

ww.Paying whenever you remember, since lend: Lenders do not wait, and a payment made after the due date can bring late fees and a credit report mark.
ww.Waiting for the lender to send a second: Waiting for a second notice means the bill is already late, so fees and credit damage may already have been triggered.
ww.Paying only when you have extra money le: Paying only when money is left over is unreliable and often leads to missed due dates, which cost fees and credit score points.

rw: Receipts and statements back up income and deductions if the IRS asks, so keeping them is a sound habit for tax purposes.

ww.Photos of meals from restaurants and caf: Photos of restaurant meals do not support income or deductions on a tax return, so they have no tax purpose.
ww.Brochures from stores you never bought f: Brochures from stores where you never bought anything document no income or expense, so they have no use for tax records.
ww.Menus from places that you visited in th: Menus from places visited are souvenirs that prove no deductible expense or income, so they do not help for tax purposes.

rw: You may be held responsible for any use of the card and PIN, and lending it can void the fraud protection you would otherwise have.

ww.Friends are not allowed by law to use an: The law does not make it illegal for a friend to use your card; the real concern is that you lose protections and take on risk.
ww.Banks charge a fee each time that a card: Banks do not generally charge a fee for sharing a card, though doing so can break the account agreement and cost you protection.
ww.The card will stop working if another pe: The card keeps working when another person touches it, so this is false, and the real risk is financial, not technical.

rw: Checking your report regularly lets you spot errors or signs of identity theft early, such as accounts you never opened.

ww.To pay a fee to the credit bureaus each: Credit bureaus must give you a free report regularly, so paying a fee each year is not a reason to check it.
ww.To raise your score each time you look a: Looking at your own report does not raise the score, since checking it is a soft inquiry that has no effect.
ww.To find out how much money your neighbor: A credit report shows your own credit history only, and it does not reveal what neighbors earn or owe.

rw: Automating transfers to savings on payday moves the money before you can spend it, which builds the habit without relying on willpower.

ww.Wait until debts are paid off to save: Waiting until debts are paid off delays saving, which leaves you without a cushion and misses years of compounding growth.
ww.Save only what is left over at month end: Saving only what is left at month end often leaves nothing, since spending expands, so saving should come first and not last.
ww.Keep all savings in cash at home in a dr: Cash kept in a drawer at home earns no interest and can be lost, stolen or burned, and it is easy to spend.

rw: Checking that you can afford the payments within your budget keeps the purchase from causing missed payments, extra interest or lasting debt.

ww.Buy it first and plan the payments later: Buying first and planning payments later risks debt you cannot afford, so planning should come before the purchase instead.
ww.Choose the longest term to make the mont: A long term lowers the monthly payment but raises the total interest, so it can hide a purchase you cannot afford.
ww.Pay the minimum and hope that your incom: Paying the minimum and hoping income rises leaves the balance and interest growing, which is a risky plan built on a guess.
